facts.answer: I can help with coding questions, explain concepts, debug errors, and answer questions about languages, tools, and frameworks. Just ask me anything coding-related!

To create a new local repo: `git init` in your project folder. To also create it on GitHub: `gh repo create` (GitHub CLI) or create it on github.com first, then `git remote add origin <url>` and `git push -u origin main`. If starting fresh: `mkdir myproject && cd myproject && git init && git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/myproject.git`

Essential git commands: `git init` (new repo), `git clone <url>` (copy repo), `git status` (see changes), `git add .` (stage all), `git add <file>` (stage one), `git commit -m 'msg'` (save snapshot), `git push` (send to remote), `git pull` (get remote changes), `git branch` (list branches), `git checkout -b name` (create+switch branch), `git merge name` (merge branch), `git log --oneline` (compact history), `git diff` (see unstaged changes), `git stash` (save work temporarily), `git stash pop` (restore stashed work)

Connect a local repo to GitHub: `git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo.git` then `git push -u origin main`. Check remotes: `git remote -v`. Change remote URL: `git remote set-url origin <new-url>`. Remove remote: `git remote remove origin`.

First push to a new remote: `git push -u origin main`. The `-u` sets the upstream so future pushes just need `git push`. If you get 'rejected' because the remote has commits you don't have: `git pull --rebase origin main` then `git push`.

Clone a repo: `git clone https://github.com/username/repo.git`. This creates a folder with the repo name. Clone into current folder: `git clone <url> .`. Clone a specific branch: `git clone -b branchname <url>`. In Termux: clone into `~/github-projects/` to keep things organized.

Save changes: `git add .` to stage everything, then `git commit -m 'your message'`. Good commit messages: describe WHAT changed and WHY. Conventional format: `feat: add login page`, `fix: broken button`, `refactor: clean up auth`, `docs: update README`. Amend last commit message: `git commit --amend -m 'new message'`. Amend and add forgotten files: `git add forgotten.js && git commit --amend --no-edit`.

Branches let you work on features without affecting main. Create and switch: `git checkout -b feature-name` (old way) or `git switch -c feature-name` (new way). Switch to existing: `git checkout main` or `git switch main`. List all branches: `git branch -a`. Delete branch: `git branch -d feature-name`. Merge branch into current: `git merge feature-name`. See what branch you're on: `git status` (shows it at the top).

`git pull` fetches and merges remote changes into your current branch. If you get merge conflicts: resolve them manually, then `git add .` and `git commit`. Safer alternative: `git pull --rebase` (replays your commits on top of the fetched commits — cleaner history). To just fetch without merging: `git fetch`.

Merge conflicts happen when two branches changed the same lines. Git marks them like this: `<<<<<<< HEAD` (your changes) `=======` (divider) `>>>>>>> branch-name` (their changes). To fix: edit the file to keep what you want, remove the markers, then `git add .` and `git commit`. VS Code and most editors have visual merge conflict tools. Abort a merge: `git merge --abort`.

`.gitignore` tells git which files to never track. Common patterns: `node_modules/` (npm packages), `.env` (secrets), `*.log` (log files), `dist/` (build output), `.DS_Store` (Mac metadata), `config.js` (sensitive config). Create it: `touch .gitignore` then edit. Files already tracked won't be ignored — untrack them first: `git rm --cached filename`. Global gitignore for all repos: `git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global`.

git init: Initialize a new Git repository in the current directory. Creates a .git folder with all necessary Git metadata. Usage: git init. After this, you can git add, git commit, and manage your project's version history.

git clone <url>: Copy a remote repository to your local machine. Downloads the entire project history. Usage: git clone https://github.com/user/repo.git. Creates a folder named after the repo and sets up the origin remote automatically.

git add: Stage files for commit. git add . stages all changes. git add <file> stages a specific file. git add -p stages changes interactively, line by line. Staging tells Git which changes you want to include in the next commit.

git commit -m 'message': Save staged changes to the repository with a descriptive message. The message explains the 'why' not just the 'what'. Good commit messages are crucial for collaboration. Use git commit --amend to modify the last commit.

git push: Upload your local commits to the remote repository (usually origin/main). First time: git push -u origin branch-name sets up tracking. git push origin <branch> pushes a specific branch. git push --all pushes all branches. Always pull before pushing to avoid conflicts.

git pull: Fetch and merge changes from the remote repository. Equivalent to git fetch followed by git merge. Always pull before starting work or before pushing. If there are conflicts, resolve them manually, then git add and git commit.

git merge <branch>: Combine changes from another branch into the current branch. First switch to the target branch (git checkout main), then git merge feature-branch. Conflicts may occur if changes overlap—resolve manually and commit the merge.

git rebase <branch>: Reapply commits on top of another branch. Cleaner history than merge, but rewrites commit history—never rebase public/shared branches. Usage: git rebase main rebases current branch onto main. Use git rebase -i for interactive rebasing (squashing, reordering commits).

git stash: Save uncommitted changes temporarily without committing. Useful when you need to switch branches but aren't ready to commit. git stash list shows saved stashes. git stash pop retrieves the most recent stash. git stash drop deletes a stash.

git log: View commit history. git log --oneline shows compact log. git log --graph --all --decorate shows a visual branch graph. git log -p shows diffs for each commit. git log --author=name filters by author. Ctrl+Q exits the log viewer.

git diff: Show changes between commits/branches. git diff shows unstaged changes. git diff --staged shows staged changes. git diff HEAD shows all changes since last commit. git diff branch1 branch2 compares two branches. git diff commit1 commit2 shows changes between commits.

git reset: Undo changes. git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes last commit, keeps changes staged. git reset --mixed HEAD~1 undoes commit, unstages changes. git reset --hard HEAD~1 undoes commit AND discards changes (dangerous!). git reset <file> unstages a file.

git cherry-pick <commit>: Apply a specific commit from another branch to the current branch. Useful for backporting fixes. git cherry-pick <commit1> <commit2> applies multiple commits. If conflicts occur, resolve them and git cherry-pick --continue.

Merge conflict: Occurs when two branches modify the same lines differently. Git marks conflicts with <<<<<<< HEAD, =======, >>>>>>>. Manually edit files to resolve (keep changes you want, delete markers), then git add and git commit. Use git mergetool for visual merge tools.

Pull request (PR): Proposed changes on GitHub/GitLab. Fork the repo, create a branch, commit changes, push, then open a PR. Allows code review before merging. Merge conflicts must be resolved before merging. Squash commits before merging keeps history clean.

Bash variables: Store data. Set with VAR=value (no spaces). Access with $VAR or ${VAR}. Quotes: single quotes preserve literal strings; double quotes allow variable expansion. Example: name='John'; echo "Hello $name" outputs 'Hello John'. Use readonly VAR=value to prevent changes.

Bash loops: for loop: for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done. for file in *.txt; do cat $file; done processes all .txt files. while loop: while condition; do commands; done. until loop: until condition; do commands; done. Loop control: break exits loop, continue skips iteration.

Bash conditionals: if [ condition ]; then commands; fi. elif and else for multiple branches. Common tests: [ -f file ] (file exists), [ -d dir ] (directory exists), [ $x -eq $y ] (equal), [ $x -gt $y ] (greater than), [ -z $var ] (empty), [ -n $var ] (not empty). Use [[ ]] for advanced patterns.

Bash functions: Define with fname() { commands; }. Call with fname [args]. Access arguments: $1, $2, $#, $@, $*. Return values: use return N (exit code 0-255). Capture output: result=$(fname). Local variables: local var=value. Functions are powerful for code reuse and modularity.

Bash pipes (|): Chain commands—output of one feeds into input of next. Example: cat file.txt | grep 'pattern' | wc -l counts matching lines. ls -la | head -20 shows first 20 files. Combine with common tools: grep (filter), sed (transform), awk (parse), sort, uniq, wc, cut.

Bash redirects: > overwrites output to file. >> appends to file. < reads input from file. 2> redirects errors to file. 2>&1 merges errors into stdout. Example: command > out.txt 2>&1 saves both output and errors. /dev/null discards output: command > /dev/null 2>&1.

chmod: Change file permissions. chmod +x file makes executable. chmod 755 rwxr-xr-x (owner read/write/execute, others read/execute). chmod 644 rw-r--r-- (owner read/write, others read). chmod -R applies recursively to directories. u=user, g=group, o=others, a=all; r=read, w=write, x=execute.

Cron: Schedule recurring tasks. crontab -e edits your crontab. Format: minute hour day month weekday command. Example: 0 12 * * * script.sh runs daily at noon. 0 */6 * * * runs every 6 hours. */5 * * * * runs every 5 minutes. Check logs with grep CRON /var/log/syslog.

Virtual environment (venv): Isolates Python projects. Create: python3 -m venv myenv. Activate: source myenv/bin/activate (Linux/Mac) or myenv\Scripts\activate (Windows). Install packages in venv: pip install package. Deactivate: deactivate. Benefits: no dependency conflicts, reproducible environments, clean pip list.

pip: Python package manager. pip install package installs from PyPI. pip install package==1.2.3 specifies version. pip install -r requirements.txt installs from file (format: package==version, one per line). pip freeze > requirements.txt exports installed packages. pip uninstall package removes packages.

F-strings (Python 3.6+): f'text {variable}' embeds expressions. Example: f'Hello {name}!' or f'{x * 2}'. Inline expressions: f'{value:>10}' right-align to 10 chars, f'{price:.2f}' format to 2 decimals. f'{name!r}' adds quotes (repr). Much more readable than % formatting or .format().

List comprehensions: [expr for item in list if condition]. Example: [x*2 for x in range(10)] generates [0, 2, 4, ..., 18]. [x for x in nums if x > 5] filters. Nested: [[x+y for x in range(3)] for y in range(3)]. Dict comprehensions: {k: v for k, v in items}. Much faster than for loops.

argparse: Parse command-line arguments. import argparse; parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(); parser.add_argument('--name', required=True); args = parser.parse_args(). Access with args.name. Supports positional args, options, defaults, help text, type conversion. Makes CLI tools professional and user-friendly.

JSON in Python: import json. json.dumps(obj) converts Python object to JSON string. json.loads(string) parses JSON string to Python object. json.dump(obj, file) writes to file. json.load(file) reads from file. Handles: dict, list, str, int, float, bool, None. Common in APIs and data storage.

requests library: HTTP requests in Python. import requests. response = requests.get(url) fetches. response.status_code, response.text, response.json(). requests.post(url, json=data) sends data. requests.headers = {'Authorization': 'Bearer token'} sets headers. Essential for APIs and web scraping.

Termux pkg commands: pkg update updates package list. pkg upgrade upgrades all packages. pkg install package installs package. pkg search query searches packages. pkg show package shows package info. apt (Debian) also works: apt-get install. Common packages: python3, nodejs, git, curl, wget, vim, openssh, ffmpeg.

Termux storage access: /storage/emulated/0 (internal storage, symlink to $HOME/storage). $HOME/storage/downloads, .../pictures, .../documents. Grant permissions: termux-setup-storage. Termux:API app required for advanced access. /data/data/com.termux/files/home is Termux home (~). Slower than native filesystem but necessary for Android integration.

Termux:API (requires app): termux-notification, termux-vibrate, termux-sensor-list. termux-battery-status shows battery info. termux-wifi-connectioninfo shows WiFi. termux-contact-list lists contacts. termux-sms-send sends SMS. termux-call-log shows call history. Install with: pkg install termux-api. Powerful for automation and scripting.

SSH key generation: ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 creates RSA key pair. -t ed25519 creates Ed25519 (modern, faster). Keys saved to ~/.ssh/id_rsa (private, keep secret!) and ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub (public, share). chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa sets correct permissions. Add public key to server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys for passwordless login.

SSH config file (~/.ssh/config): Define hosts for easy access. Example: Host github.com / HostName github.com / User git / IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_rsa. Then ssh github.com works seamlessly. Port forwarding: Host=github.com / LocalForward 3306 remote.db.server:3306 tunnels remote MySQL locally.

Environment variables: export VAR=value sets variable for subprocess. $PATH is colon-separated list of directories to search for commands. export PATH="$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin" adds to PATH. Use ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile to make permanent. env shows all variables. unset VAR removes. $HOME, $USER, $PWD, $?, $! are special variables.

.env files: Store sensitive config (API keys, passwords, database URLs) without committing to Git. Format: KEY=value. In Python: from dotenv import load_dotenv; load_dotenv() then os.getenv('KEY'). In bash: source .env then use $KEY. Add .env to .gitignore. Never commit secrets!

Reading stack traces: Error message at bottom, shows what went wrong. Traceback above shows call sequence—topmost frame is where error originated, bottom is where exception was thrown. Look for YOUR code in the trace (skip library internals). Line numbers tell you exactly where to look. For segfaults: use gdb or valgrind.

Syntax errors: Code structure is invalid (missing colon, bracket, quote, etc.). Compiler/interpreter stops immediately and points to error location. Common Python mistakes: missing colon after if/for/def, indentation errors, unclosed parentheses. Use linters (flake8, pylint) to catch before running.

Null pointer error (C/C++): Dereferencing a null pointer (address 0) crashes. Use debuggers: gdb program, then run, then print variable. valgrind program detects memory issues. In Python: AttributeError or TypeError for similar null-safety issues. Always check for None before using objects.

Regular expressions (regex): Pattern matching syntax. In Python: import re; re.match(pattern, string) matches at start, re.search finds anywhere, re.findall finds all. Pattern syntax: . (any char), * (0+ times), + (1+ times), ? (optional), [abc] (char class), ^ (start), $ (end), \d (digit), \w (word char), \s (whitespace).

JSON errors: Common: unclosed quotes, trailing commas (not allowed), single quotes (must be double), unescaped newlines. Use online JSON validators. Python: json.loads() fails on invalid JSON, shows line/char number. json.dumps() is safe if you start with valid Python objects. When working with APIs, always validate response is JSON before parsing.

curl: Command-line HTTP client. curl https://api.example.com fetches. curl -X POST -d 'data' sends POST. curl -H 'Header: value' sets headers. curl -o file.txt saves to file. curl -L follows redirects. curl -i shows headers. curl -w '%{http_code}' shows status code. Essential for API testing.

Ports: 0-1023 system ports (80=HTTP, 443=HTTPS, 22=SSH, 3306=MySQL, 5432=PostgreSQL, 6379=Redis). 1024-49151 registered (8080, 8000, 3000 common for development). 49152-65535 dynamic/private. netstat -tlnp shows listening ports. ss -tlnp modern replacement. lsof -i :port shows process on port.

localhost: 127.0.0.1 (loopback), only accessible from your machine. 0.0.0.0 binds to all network interfaces. Use localhost:8000 for development. To access from other machines: use your machine's IP (hostname -I in Linux). Firewalls may block external access. Port forwarding or reverse proxy (nginx) for production access.

In Termux, your home directory is /data/data/com.termux/files/home/ — this is what ~ expands to. So ~/github-projects/ is actually /data/data/com.termux/files/home/github-projects/. You can access Android storage at ~/storage/ after running 'termux-setup-storage'.

tmux basics: Start session: `tmux` or `tmux new -s name`. Detach: Ctrl+b then d. List sessions: `tmux ls`. Attach: `tmux attach -t name` or `tmux a`. Kill session: `tmux kill-session -t name`. Windows: Ctrl+b c (new), Ctrl+b n/p (next/prev), Ctrl+b w (list), Ctrl+b , (rename). Panes: Ctrl+b % (split vertical), Ctrl+b " (split horizontal), Ctrl+b arrow (switch), Ctrl+b z (zoom/unzoom), Ctrl+b x (kill pane). Scroll: Ctrl+b [ then arrows/PageUp (q to exit). In Termux: tmux is essential since /tmp doesn't exist — use sessions instead of background jobs.

tmux configuration (~/.tmux.conf): Change prefix: `set -g prefix C-a` (many prefer Ctrl+a over Ctrl+b). Enable mouse: `set -g mouse on`. Start windows at 1: `set -g base-index 1`. Reload config: `tmux source-file ~/.tmux.conf` or Ctrl+b then `:source-file ~/.tmux.conf`. Status bar: `set -g status-bg black` and `set -g status-fg white`. Vi keys in copy mode: `setw -g mode-keys vi`. Copy text: Ctrl+b [ to enter copy mode, v to select, y to yank, Ctrl+b ] to paste.

vim basics: Open file: `vim filename`. Modes: Normal (default, press Esc), Insert (press i to type), Visual (press v to select), Command (press : for commands). Essential: i=insert before cursor, a=insert after, o=new line below, Esc=return to normal. Navigation: h/j/k/l (left/down/up/right), w/b (word forward/back), gg=top, G=bottom, :n=line n. Save: :w. Quit: :q. Save and quit: :wq or ZZ. Quit without saving: :q!. Search: /pattern (n=next, N=prev). Replace all: :%s/old/new/g. Delete line: dd. Undo: u. Redo: Ctrl+r.

vim intermediate: Visual mode: v (char), V (line), Ctrl+v (block). Yank (copy): y (selected), yy (line), y3j (3 lines). Paste: p (after cursor), P (before). Delete: d (selected), dd (line), dw (word). Change: c (delete + insert mode), cw (change word), C (change to end of line). Indent: >> (in), << (out), = (auto-indent). Splits: :sp (horizontal), :vsp (vertical), Ctrl+w+arrow (switch). Buffers: :e file (open), :bn/:bp (next/prev), :ls (list). Marks: ma (set mark a), 'a (jump to mark a). Macros: qa (record to register a), q (stop), @a (replay), @@ (repeat last).

Python debugging: Built-in debugger: `import pdb; pdb.set_trace()` or (Python 3.7+) `breakpoint()`. pdb commands: n=next line, s=step into, c=continue, l=list code, p var=print variable, pp=pretty print, b line=set breakpoint, w=where (stack trace), q=quit. VS Code: add `"debugpy"` and set breakpoints in editor. Print debugging: f-strings are great — `print(f'{var=}')` prints name and value. logging module: better than print for production — `import logging; logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG); logging.debug('msg')`. Traceback: read bottom-up — the last line is the actual error. Common: AttributeError=wrong attribute name, TypeError=wrong type, KeyError=missing dict key, IndexError=list out of bounds.

Python error handling: try/except: `try: risky() except ValueError as e: print(e) except (TypeError, KeyError): pass else: print('no error') finally: cleanup()`. Raise: `raise ValueError('message')`. Custom exceptions: `class MyError(Exception): pass`. Logging: `import logging; logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format='%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s')`. Levels: DEBUG < INFO < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL. Log to file: `logging.basicConfig(filename='app.log', ...)`. Context managers: `with open('file') as f:` — auto-closes even on exception. Assert: `assert condition, 'message'` — raises AssertionError if false (use for development, not production).

Bash advanced: Arrays: `arr=(a b c)`, `${arr[0]}`, `${arr[@]}` (all), `${#arr[@]}` (length). Loops: `for i in {1..5}; do echo $i; done`. `while read line; do echo $line; done < file.txt`. Functions: `myfunc() { echo $1; }; myfunc arg`. String ops: `${var,,}` (lowercase), `${var^^}` (uppercase), `${var:0:5}` (substring), `${var/old/new}` (replace), `${var:-default}` (default if unset). Conditionals: `[[ $a == $b ]]`, `[[ -f file ]]` (exists), `[[ -d dir ]]` (is dir), `[[ $a =~ regex ]]`. Process substitution: `diff <(cmd1) <(cmd2)`. Heredoc: `cat <<EOF ... EOF`. Trap: `trap 'cleanup' EXIT INT`.

Bash piping and redirection: `cmd > file` (overwrite), `cmd >> file` (append), `cmd 2> err.txt` (stderr), `cmd &> all.txt` (stdout+stderr), `cmd < input.txt` (stdin). Pipe: `cmd1 | cmd2`. xargs: `find . -name '*.log' | xargs rm`. `echo 'a b c' | xargs -n1 echo`. Subshell: `(cd /tmp && ls)` — runs in subshell, doesn't affect current dir. Command substitution: `result=$(cmd)` or backticks. Background: `cmd &`, `jobs`, `fg`, `bg`. Process: `ps aux | grep name`, `kill PID`, `kill -9 PID` (force). `&&` (run if prev succeeded), `||` (run if prev failed), `;` (always run next).

Git advanced: Rebase: `git rebase main` (replay commits on top of main — cleaner history than merge). Interactive rebase: `git rebase -i HEAD~3` (edit/squash/reorder last 3 commits). Cherry-pick: `git cherry-pick abc1234` (apply specific commit to current branch). Bisect: `git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.0` — binary search for bug-introducing commit. Reflog: `git reflog` — shows all HEAD movements, recover 'lost' commits. Reset: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` (undo commit, keep staged), `--mixed` (unstage too), `--hard` (discard all changes). Worktree: `git worktree add ../feature-branch feature` — check out branch in separate folder without switching.

Git extra features: Stash: `git stash` (save dirty state), `git stash pop` (restore), `git stash list`, `git stash apply stash@{1}`, `git stash drop`. Tags: `git tag v1.0` (lightweight), `git tag -a v1.0 -m 'release'` (annotated), `git push origin v1.0`, `git push --tags`. Hooks: scripts in .git/hooks/ — pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push etc. (chmod +x to enable). Aliases: `git config --global alias.st status`. Submodules: `git submodule add <url>`, `git submodule update --init --recursive`. Sparse checkout (large repos): `git sparse-checkout set path/to/folder`.

Node.js basics: Run file: `node file.js`. REPL: `node` (interactive). npm: `npm init -y` (new project), `npm install package`, `npm install -D package` (dev dep), `npm run script`. package.json scripts: `"start": "node index.js"`, `"dev": "nodemon index.js"`. CommonJS: `const x = require('./module')`, `module.exports = x`. ES Modules: `import x from './module.js'`, `export default x`, `export { x }` — requires `"type": "module"` in package.json or .mjs extension. `__dirname` and `__filename` (CommonJS only). `process.env.VAR` for env variables. `process.argv` for CLI args. Built-in modules: fs, path, http, os, events, crypto.

Node.js async patterns: EventEmitter: `const ee = new EventEmitter(); ee.on('event', cb); ee.emit('event', data)`. Streams: `fs.createReadStream('file').pipe(process.stdout)` — memory efficient for large files. HTTP server: `http.createServer((req, res) => { res.end('Hello') }).listen(3000)`. Express: `const app = express(); app.get('/path', (req, res) => res.json({ok: true})); app.listen(3000)`. Middleware: `app.use((req, res, next) => { next() })`. Error middleware: `app.use((err, req, res, next) => res.status(500).json({error: err.message}))`. Worker threads for CPU-intensive tasks. cluster module for multi-core utilization.

SQL advanced joins and queries: INNER JOIN: only matching rows. LEFT JOIN: all left rows + matching right (nulls if no match). RIGHT JOIN: reverse. FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both. `SELECT a.*, b.name FROM orders a LEFT JOIN users b ON a.user_id = b.id`. Subqueries: `SELECT * FROM products WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)`. CTEs: `WITH cte AS (SELECT ...) SELECT * FROM cte`. Window functions: `SELECT name, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) FROM employees`. GROUP BY with HAVING: `SELECT dept, COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5`. CASE: `SELECT name, CASE WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A' ELSE 'B' END grade FROM students`.

SQL performance: EXPLAIN (MySQL) / EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL): shows query execution plan — look for full table scans (bad). Indexes: `CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table(column)` — speeds up WHERE/JOIN on that column, slows down writes. Composite index: `CREATE INDEX idx ON table(col1, col2)` — only used if col1 is in query. Avoid SELECT *: fetch only needed columns. N+1 problem: loading related records in a loop — fix with JOIN or eager loading. Transactions: `BEGIN; UPDATE ...; UPDATE ...; COMMIT;` — all-or-nothing. Connection pooling: reuse DB connections (pg-pool, HikariCP). Slow query log: enable in MySQL/PostgreSQL to catch problem queries. Normalize to reduce duplication, denormalize for read performance.

GitHub Actions basics: Create .github/workflows/ci.yml. Triggers: `on: [push, pull_request]` or `on: push: branches: [main]`. Basic workflow: `jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - uses: actions/setup-node@v4 with: node-version: '20' - run: npm ci - run: npm test`. Secrets: store in repo Settings → Secrets → use as `${{ secrets.MY_SECRET }}`. Matrix: `strategy: matrix: node: [18, 20, 22]`. Artifacts: `uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: build path: dist/`. Cache: `uses: actions/cache@v4 with: path: ~/.npm key: ${{ runner.os }}-node-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}`.

GitHub Actions advanced: Manual trigger: `on: workflow_dispatch: inputs: env: description: 'Target env' required: true`. Deploy to GitHub Pages: `uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4`. Reusable workflows: `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable.yml with: param: value`. Environment protection rules: Settings → Environments → add reviewers for production deploys. `GITHUB_TOKEN`: auto-provided, can push/create releases. Create release: `uses: actions/create-release@v1`. Conditional steps: `if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'`. Self-hosted runners: run on your own hardware. Composite actions: package multiple steps into a reusable action in action.yml.

pytest basics: Install: `pip install pytest`. Run: `pytest` (finds test_*.py files). Test function: `def test_add(): assert add(1, 2) == 3`. Run specific: `pytest test_file.py::test_function -v`. Fixtures: `@pytest.fixture def client(): return app.test_client()`. Use in test: `def test_route(client): r = client.get('/'); assert r.status_code == 200`. Parametrize: `@pytest.mark.parametrize('a,b,expected', [(1,2,3),(4,5,9)]) def test_add(a,b,expected): assert add(a,b)==expected`. Skip: `@pytest.mark.skip(reason='not ready')`. Expected exception: `with pytest.raises(ValueError): func()`. Coverage: `pip install pytest-cov; pytest --cov=myapp --cov-report=html`.

Python mocking: `from unittest.mock import Mock, patch, MagicMock`. Patch decorator: `@patch('mymodule.requests.get') def test_api(mock_get): mock_get.return_value.json.return_value = {'ok': True}`. Context manager: `with patch('module.func') as mock: mock.return_value = 42`. MagicMock: auto-creates attributes/methods on access. Assert calls: `mock.assert_called_once_with(arg)`, `mock.call_count`, `mock.call_args_list`. pytest monkeypatch: `def test_env(monkeypatch): monkeypatch.setenv('KEY', 'val')`. Mock side effects: `mock.side_effect = [1, 2, ValueError('fail')]`. Spy: `mocker.spy(obj, 'method')` (pytest-mock) — calls real function but records calls.

Regex advanced: Named groups: `(?P<name>pattern)` — access with `m.group('name')`. Non-capturing group: `(?:pattern)`. Lookahead: `foo(?=bar)` (foo followed by bar, bar not captured). Negative lookahead: `foo(?!bar)`. Lookbehind: `(?<=foo)bar`. Non-greedy: `.*?` (match as little as possible). Backreference: `(\w+) \1` matches repeated word. In Python: `re.compile(pattern, re.IGNORECASE | re.MULTILINE | re.DOTALL)`. `re.search` (first match anywhere), `re.match` (start of string), `re.findall` (all matches), `re.sub('pat', 'repl', text)`, `re.split`. Verbose mode: `re.VERBOSE` — allows whitespace and comments in pattern. Word boundary: `\b`, digit: `\d`, whitespace: `\s`, any: `.` (except newline without DOTALL).

curl advanced: POST JSON: `curl -X POST https://api.example.com/data -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"key":"value"}'`. Auth: `curl -u user:pass URL` (basic), `curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer TOKEN' URL`. Save to file: `curl -o output.html URL`. Silent: `curl -s URL`. Follow redirects: `curl -L URL`. Show headers: `curl -I URL` (HEAD only), `curl -v URL` (verbose). Upload file: `curl -F 'file=@path/to/file' URL`. Cookies: `curl -b cookies.txt -c cookies.txt URL`. Rate info: `curl -w '%{time_total}\n' -o /dev/null -s URL`. Multiple URLs: `curl URL1 URL2`. Retry: `curl --retry 3 --retry-delay 2 URL`.

find command: `find /path -name '*.js'` (by name), `-iname` (case-insensitive). By type: `-type f` (file), `-type d` (dir), `-type l` (symlink). By size: `-size +1M` (over 1MB), `-size -100k`. By time: `-mtime -7` (modified in last 7 days), `-newer file.txt`. By permission: `-perm 644`. Execute: `find . -name '*.log' -exec rm {} \;` or `-exec rm {} +` (batched, faster). Print: `-print0` (null-separated, safe for spaces). Exclude dir: `-not -path '*/node_modules/*'`. Combine: `find . -name '*.py' -not -name '__init__.py'`. Depth: `-maxdepth 2`. In Termux: find works normally but some system paths are restricted.

grep advanced: Recursive: `grep -r 'pattern' .` or `-R` (follow symlinks). Case insensitive: `-i`. Show line numbers: `-n`. Count matches: `-c`. Only filenames: `-l`. Invert match: `-v`. Extended regex: `-E` (enables +, ?, |, ()). Perl regex: `-P` (enables \d, \w, lookaheads). Context: `-A 3` (3 lines after), `-B 3` (before), `-C 3` (both). Color: `--color=always`. Fixed string (no regex): `-F`. Word boundary: `-w`. Multiple patterns: `-e 'pat1' -e 'pat2'`. Exclude: `--exclude='*.log'`, `--exclude-dir=node_modules`. ripgrep (rg): faster alternative — `rg 'pattern'` — respects .gitignore by default, faster than grep. `rg -t js 'pattern'` (only .js files).

sed and awk: sed (stream editor): `sed 's/old/new/g' file` (replace all in file), `sed -i 's/old/new/g' file` (in-place). `sed -n '5,10p' file` (print lines 5-10). `sed '/pattern/d' file` (delete matching lines). `sed 's/^/prefix/' file` (add prefix to each line). awk: `awk '{print $1}' file` (first field). `awk -F',' '{print $2}' file` (comma-separated). `awk 'NR>1' file` (skip header). `awk '{sum+=$1} END{print sum}' file` (sum column). `awk '/pattern/{print $0}' file` (filter). `awk '{print $NF}' file` (last field). Combine: `cat file | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` (frequency count of first column).

Environment variables: Set in shell: `export MY_VAR=value` (current session). Persistent: add to ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile. Check: `echo $MY_VAR`, `env | grep MY`, `printenv MY_VAR`. Unset: `unset MY_VAR`. .env files: create `.env` with `KEY=value` lines — never commit to git (add to .gitignore!). In Node.js: `require('dotenv').config()` then `process.env.KEY`. In Python: `from dotenv import load_dotenv; load_dotenv(); os.getenv('KEY')`. In bash: `set -a; source .env; set +a`. System-wide: /etc/environment (Ubuntu). Default value: `${MY_VAR:-default}`. Required check in bash: `${MY_VAR:?'MY_VAR is required'}` — exits with error if unset.

proot-distro: Run full Linux distros inside Termux without root. Install: `pkg install proot-distro`. List available: `proot-distro list`. Install Ubuntu: `proot-distro install ubuntu`. Login: `proot-distro login ubuntu`. Login as root: `proot-distro login ubuntu --user root`. Inside the distro: full apt, systemd-style packages, /tmp works, standard Linux paths. Exit: `exit`. Remove: `proot-distro remove ubuntu`. Backup: `proot-distro backup ubuntu > ubuntu.tar.gz`. Restore: `proot-distro restore < ubuntu.tar.gz`. Useful for: running tools that need /tmp, glibc binaries, Python packages with compiled C extensions, development environments that expect standard Linux paths. Note: no real root — kernel calls go through proot.

JavaScript async/await: async function always returns a Promise. await pauses execution until Promise resolves — can only use inside async function. `async function fetchUser(id) { const res = await fetch('/api/users/' + id); const data = await res.json(); return data; }`. Error handling: `try { const data = await fetchUser(1) } catch (err) { console.error(err) }`. Parallel: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetch(url1), fetch(url2)])` — runs concurrently. Promise.allSettled: waits for all, doesn't reject on failure. Promise.race: resolves/rejects with first to settle. Promise.any: resolves with first success. Chaining: `fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(data => ...).catch(err => ...)`. Convert callback to promise: `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { cb(err => err ? reject(err) : resolve()) })`.

TypeScript basics: Superset of JavaScript — adds static types. Install: `npm install -D typescript tsx`. Run: `npx tsx file.ts` or compile with `tsc`. Basic types: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `any` (avoid), `unknown` (safer than any), `never` (never returns). Interfaces: `interface User { id: number; name: string; email?: string }` (? = optional). Type aliases: `type ID = string | number`. Generics: `function identity<T>(arg: T): T { return arg }`. Arrays: `string[]` or `Array<string>`. Union: `string | number`. Intersection: `TypeA & TypeB`. Type narrowing: `if (typeof x === 'string') { ... }`. Readonly: `readonly id: number`. tsconfig.json: `"strict": true` catches most bugs.

Writing good commit messages: Conventional Commits format: `type(scope): description`. Types: feat (new feature), fix (bug fix), refactor (code change, no behavior change), docs (documentation), test (adding tests), style (formatting), chore (maintenance), perf (performance). Examples: `feat(auth): add JWT token refresh`, `fix(login): prevent double-submit on slow networks`, `refactor: extract payment logic into service`. Rules: subject line ≤ 72 chars, imperative mood ('add' not 'added'), no period at end. Body: explain WHY not WHAT (the diff shows what). Footer: `BREAKING CHANGE: ...` or `Closes #123`. Avoid: 'fixed stuff', 'wip', 'asdf'. Atomic commits: one logical change per commit — easier to review, bisect, and revert.

Debugging strategies: Read the error message fully — the last line is the actual error, the stack trace shows where. Reproduce reliably before trying to fix. Rubber duck debugging: explain your code line-by-line out loud (or to a duck) — you often find the bug before finishing. Bisect: comment out half the code to find which half has the bug. Print/log strategically: log inputs and outputs at function boundaries. Check assumptions: `assert len(data) > 0, 'data is empty'`. Minimal reproduction: strip down to the smallest code that still shows the bug. Read docs: most bugs are misunderstandings of how a function behaves. Google the exact error message in quotes. Take breaks: fresh eyes catch things tired eyes miss. Version control: `git diff` shows exactly what changed since it last worked.

JavaScript modules: ES Modules (modern): `export const x = 1`, `export default function() {}`, `import { x } from './module.js'`, `import fn from './module.js'`. Dynamic import: `const mod = await import('./module.js')` — lazy loading. CommonJS (Node.js legacy): `module.exports = { x }`, `const { x } = require('./module')`. Bundlers: Vite (fast, uses native ES modules in dev), Webpack (mature, very configurable), esbuild (extremely fast, used by Vite under the hood), Rollup (great for libraries). Tree shaking: bundlers remove unused exports — only works with ES modules. Import maps (browser native): `<script type='importmap'>` to map bare imports without a bundler. Barrel files: `index.js` that re-exports from multiple files — can hurt tree shaking if not careful.

In mj CLI, I can create CSV files for you — just say 'make me a file called data.csv'. For full spreadsheet features like Excel formulas and formatting, you'd use LibreOffice Calc, Google Sheets, or Microsoft Excel. I can also help you write Python scripts using pandas or openpyxl to create/manipulate spreadsheets programmatically.

HTML5 semantic elements describe meaning, not just style: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<section>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<figure>`, `<figcaption>`, `<time>`, `<mark>`. Help screen readers, SEO, and code readability. Use `<article>` for self-contained content (blog post), `<section>` for thematic groupings, `<aside>` for tangential content.

Flexbox is one-dimensional layout. Parent: `display: flex`, `flex-direction: row|column`, `justify-content` (main axis: flex-start, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly), `align-items` (cross axis: stretch, center, flex-start, flex-end, baseline), `flex-wrap: wrap`, `gap: 1rem`. Children: `flex: 1` (grow), `flex: 0 0 200px` (fixed), `align-self`, `order`.

CSS Grid is two-dimensional layout. `display: grid`, `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr` or `repeat(3, 1fr)` or `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr))`. `grid-template-rows`, `gap: 1rem`. Place items: `grid-column: 1 / 3` (span columns), `grid-row: 2 / 4`. Named areas: `grid-template-areas: 'header header' 'nav main' 'footer footer'`. Auto-fit vs auto-fill: auto-fit collapses empty tracks.

CSS custom properties (variables): `:root { --primary: #3b82f6; --space: 1rem; }`. Use: `color: var(--primary)`. Cascading and inheritable — unlike Sass vars (compile-time). Fallback: `var(--missing, red)`. Update at runtime via JS: `el.style.setProperty('--primary', 'blue')`. Great for theming (dark mode toggle: swap variables on `:root`).

CSS animations: `@keyframes fadeIn { from { opacity: 0 } to { opacity: 1 } }` then `animation: fadeIn 0.3s ease-in-out`. Properties: `animation-name`, `-duration`, `-timing-function` (ease, ease-in, ease-out, linear, cubic-bezier), `-delay`, `-iteration-count` (number or `infinite`), `-direction` (normal, reverse, alternate), `-fill-mode` (forwards keeps end state). Prefer `transform` and `opacity` for GPU acceleration.

Media queries: `@media (max-width: 768px) { ... }`. Common breakpoints: 640px (sm), 768px (md), 1024px (lg), 1280px (xl). Mobile-first: write base styles for mobile, use `min-width` to add styles for larger screens. Other features: `prefers-color-scheme: dark`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `orientation: landscape`, `hover: hover` (true mouse vs touch).

Mobile-first design: write base CSS for small screens, then progressively enhance with `min-width` media queries for larger screens. Why: forces you to prioritize content; mobile is ~60% of web traffic; smaller stylesheets load first. Pattern: `.card { padding: 1rem } @media (min-width: 768px) { .card { padding: 2rem } }`.

Sass (SCSS syntax) extends CSS: variables (`$primary: blue`), nesting (`.card { &:hover { ... } }`), mixins (`@mixin button { ... } .btn { @include button }`), functions, partials (`_buttons.scss` imported with `@use`), math operators. Compiles to plain CSS. Modern CSS now has variables and nesting (browser-native), reducing Sass's necessity for many projects.

Tailwind CSS: utility-first framework. Compose styles with classes like `flex items-center gap-4 px-6 py-3 bg-blue-500 hover:bg-blue-600 text-white rounded-lg`. JIT compiler scans your files and only generates classes you use — small output. Config: `tailwind.config.js` for theme tokens. Best with `@apply` for repeated patterns: `.btn { @apply px-4 py-2 rounded }`. Tradeoff: HTML gets verbose.

Bootstrap: opinionated component framework (since 2011 by Twitter). Grid system (12 columns: `col-md-6`), pre-styled components (buttons, cards, modals, navbars), JavaScript widgets (carousel, dropdown). Easy to start, hard to customize without overrides. Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery. Compared to Tailwind: Bootstrap = ready-made UI; Tailwind = build your own UI with utilities.

DOM manipulation: `document.querySelector('.btn')` (first match), `querySelectorAll` (NodeList). Modify: `el.textContent = 'hi'`, `el.innerHTML = 'hi'` (XSS risk if untrusted), `el.classList.add/remove/toggle('active')`, `el.style.color = 'red'`. Create: `document.createElement('div')`, `parent.appendChild(child)`, `el.remove()`. Attributes: `getAttribute`, `setAttribute`, `dataset.userId` for `data-user-id`.

JavaScript events: `el.addEventListener('click', (e) => { ... })`. Common: click, input, change, submit, keydown, mouseenter, scroll, load, DOMContentLoaded. Event object: `e.target` (clicked element), `e.currentTarget` (listener element), `e.preventDefault()` (stop default), `e.stopPropagation()` (stop bubbling). Delegation: attach one listener to parent, use `e.target.closest('.btn')` to handle child clicks — efficient for dynamic lists.

Promises represent eventual completion: `new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })`. States: pending → fulfilled or rejected. Chain: `.then(value => ...).catch(err => ...).finally(() => ...)`. Combine: `Promise.all([p1, p2])` (all or first rejection), `Promise.allSettled` (waits for all), `Promise.race` (first to settle), `Promise.any` (first fulfilled). Prefer async/await for readability.

A closure is a function that remembers its enclosing scope, even after that scope has returned. `function makeCounter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n }`. Each call to `makeCounter()` creates a new `n` captured by the inner function. Used for: data privacy, factory functions, memoization, event handler state. Beware: closures over loop variables — use `let` (block-scoped) not `var` (function-scoped).

JavaScript inheritance is prototype-based: every object has an internal `[[Prototype]]` (accessed via `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` or `__proto__`). Property lookup walks up the chain. `class` syntax is sugar over prototypes. `Object.create(proto)` makes a new object with given prototype. `Array.prototype.map` is why all arrays have `.map`. Modify prototypes only on your own classes — patching built-ins (`Array.prototype.foo = ...`) breaks libraries.

ES6 classes: `class User { constructor(name) { this.name = name } greet() { return 'hi ' + this.name } }`. Inheritance: `class Admin extends User { constructor(n) { super(n); this.role = 'admin' } }`. Static methods: `static fromJSON(s) { ... }`. Private fields: `#password`. Getters/setters: `get fullName() { return ... }`. Under the hood: still prototypes.

Destructuring: `const { name, age } = user`, `const [first, second, ...rest] = arr`. Rename: `const { name: userName } = user`. Defaults: `const { name = 'anon' } = user`. Nested: `const { addr: { city } } = user`. Function params: `function greet({ name, age = 0 }) { ... }`. Swap: `[a, b] = [b, a]`. Skip array: `const [, second] = arr`.

Spread `...` expands iterables/objects. Array: `[...a, ...b]` (concat), `[...new Set(arr)]` (dedupe), `Math.max(...nums)`. Object: `{ ...user, age: 30 }` (shallow merge — later wins). Function calls: `fn(...args)`. Rest collects: `function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((a,b) => a+b, 0) }`, `const [first, ...rest] = arr`. Shallow copy — nested objects share references.

Optional chaining `?.` short-circuits to undefined if any link is null/undefined: `user?.address?.city`. Methods: `arr?.[0]`, `fn?.()`. Combine with nullish coalescing: `user?.name ?? 'anon'`. Don't overuse — if a property should exist, let it throw so you catch bugs early. Doesn't help with property access on `undefined`-as-error-state.

Nullish coalescing `??` returns right side only if left is null or undefined (NOT for 0, '', or false). `const port = config.port ?? 3000` — keeps `0` as valid value. Compare to `||` which also falls back on 0, '', false. Combine: `user?.name ?? 'anon'`. Assignment: `x ??= 5` sets only if x is nullish.

Web Components: framework-free reusable components. Three pieces: Custom Elements (`class MyEl extends HTMLElement { connectedCallback() { ... } } customElements.define('my-el', MyEl)`), Shadow DOM (encapsulated styles/markup: `this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' })`), HTML Templates (`<template>`). Use: design systems shared across frameworks. Limitations: form participation, SSR are still rough.

Service Workers: background scripts that proxy network requests, enabling offline support and caching. Lifecycle: install → activate → fetch. Register: `navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')`. Cache: `caches.open('v1').then(c => c.addAll(['/index.html', '/app.js']))`. Strategies: cache-first (offline-first), network-first (fresh content), stale-while-revalidate. Must be HTTPS (localhost OK).

PWA: web app that feels native. Requirements: HTTPS, manifest.json (name, icons, theme_color, display: 'standalone'), service worker for offline. Installable via 'Add to Home Screen'. Features: push notifications, background sync, offline mode, app-like UI. Tools: Workbox (Google's service-worker library), Lighthouse (audit). Examples: Twitter Lite, Starbucks, Pinterest.

WebSockets: persistent full-duplex connection over TCP. Browser: `const ws = new WebSocket('wss://example.com'); ws.onmessage = e => ...; ws.send('hi')`. Server: Node's `ws` library, Socket.IO (adds reconnection, rooms, fallback). Use for: chat, multiplayer games, live dashboards, collaborative editing. Alternatives: SSE (Server-Sent Events, one-way), long polling, HTTP/2 push (deprecated).

WebRTC: browser-to-browser real-time audio/video/data, no server in the data path. Components: `RTCPeerConnection` (the connection), `getUserMedia` (camera/mic access), data channels (P2P arbitrary data). Needs a signaling server (often WebSocket) to exchange SDP offers and ICE candidates. STUN/TURN servers help with NAT traversal. Use: video chat, file sharing, multiplayer games.

Canvas API: bitmap drawing surface. `<canvas id='c' width='800' height='600'>`, `const ctx = c.getContext('2d')`. Methods: `fillRect`, `strokeRect`, `beginPath`, `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `arc`, `fill`, `stroke`, `drawImage`, `fillText`. Pixel data: `getImageData`, `putImageData`. No DOM events on shapes — track manually. For 3D: `getContext('webgl')` or `webgl2`. For complex scenes: Three.js, PixiJS, Phaser.

SVG: XML-based vector graphics, scale infinitely. Inline: `<svg viewBox='0 0 100 100'><circle cx='50' cy='50' r='40' fill='red'/></svg>`. Elements: rect, circle, ellipse, line, polyline, polygon, path. `path d='M 10 10 L 90 10 L 50 90 Z'` (Move, Line, Close). Style with CSS, animate with CSS or SMIL. Great for icons (much smaller than PNG), charts (D3.js).

Web Audio API: graph-based audio synthesis/processing. `const ctx = new AudioContext(); const osc = ctx.createOscillator(); osc.frequency.value = 440; osc.connect(ctx.destination); osc.start()`. Nodes: oscillator, gain, filter, delay, convolver (reverb), analyser (frequency data for visualizations). Load samples: `decodeAudioData` then `createBufferSource`. Latency-critical apps: schedule via `currentTime + offset`, not `setTimeout`.

WebGL: low-level 3D graphics in browser (OpenGL ES 2.0/3.0 bindings). You write GLSL shaders (vertex + fragment) and manage buffers/textures/uniforms manually. Very verbose. Use Three.js for almost everything — it wraps WebGL with scenes, cameras, meshes, materials. WebGPU is the modern successor: better API, compute shaders, broader hardware support.

Three.js: 3D rendering library on top of WebGL. Core: Scene, Camera (Perspective or Orthographic), Renderer. Objects: Mesh = Geometry + Material. Materials: MeshBasicMaterial (no lighting), MeshStandardMaterial (PBR), MeshPhongMaterial. Lights: AmbientLight, DirectionalLight, PointLight. Loaders: GLTFLoader for models. Animate via `requestAnimationFrame` loop, update `mesh.rotation.y`, call `renderer.render(scene, camera)`.

React Hooks let function components hold state and side effects. `useState(initial)` returns [value, setter]. `useEffect(() => { ... return () => cleanup() }, [deps])` runs after render; cleanup runs before next effect or unmount. Rules: only call at top level (no conditionals/loops), only in components or other hooks. Empty deps = run once. No deps = every render. Reactive deps = run when they change.

`useContext(MyContext)` reads value from nearest `<MyContext.Provider value={...}>`. Create: `const ThemeContext = createContext('light')`. Re-renders all consumers when Provider value changes — split contexts to avoid wasted renders. Good for: theme, user, locale. Bad for: high-frequency updates (cursor position, animations) — use a state library instead.

`useReducer(reducer, initial)` for complex state. `reducer(state, action) => newState`. Returns `[state, dispatch]`. `dispatch({ type: 'INCREMENT', payload: 1 })`. Better than useState when: state has multiple sub-values, next state depends on previous, transitions are complex. Use immer for ergonomic immutable updates.

`useMemo(() => expensiveCompute(a, b), [a, b])` caches a value across renders, recomputing only when deps change. Use for: expensive calculations, stable object/array references passed to memoized children. Don't wrap everything — memoization itself has cost. Profile first. Common pattern: `const sorted = useMemo(() => items.sort(...), [items])`.

`useCallback(fn, deps)` returns a memoized callback — same reference until deps change. Equivalent to `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Use when passing callbacks to memoized children (React.memo) to avoid unnecessary re-renders. Otherwise the wrapper costs more than it saves. Common with effect deps: stable callback prevents effect from firing every render.

`useRef(initial)`: mutable container that persists across renders without causing re-renders. `const inputRef = useRef(null); <input ref={inputRef} />; inputRef.current.focus()`. Also for: storing previous values, mutable counters, holding interval IDs. Updating `.current` does NOT trigger render — use useState if you need re-render.

React Router (v6+): client-side routing. `<BrowserRouter><Routes><Route path='/' element={<Home/>}/><Route path='/users/:id' element={<User/>}/></Routes></BrowserRouter>`. Hooks: `useParams()` for URL params, `useNavigate()` to programmatically navigate, `useLocation()` for current URL, `useSearchParams()` for query string. Nested routes via `<Outlet/>`. Data Router (v6.4+): loaders/actions for data fetching.

Redux: predictable state container. Single store, reducers (pure functions: `(state, action) => newState`), actions (plain objects). Modern Redux = Redux Toolkit (RTK): `createSlice` generates reducers + action creators; `createAsyncThunk` for async; `configureStore` sets up store + devtools + thunk. RTK Query for data fetching. Most React apps don't need Redux — try React Context + useReducer or Zustand first.

Next.js: React framework with SSR, SSG, ISR, file-based routing, image optimization, API routes. App Router (v13+, default): React Server Components by default, `'use client'` to opt into client; `app/page.tsx`, `layout.tsx`, `loading.tsx`, `error.tsx`. Pages Router (legacy): `pages/` directory with `getServerSideProps`, `getStaticProps`. Deploy: Vercel (creator), or self-host as Node server / static export.

Vue.js: progressive JavaScript framework. Single-file components: `.vue` files with `<template>`, `<script>`, `<style>`. Vue 3 Composition API: `<script setup>`, `ref`, `reactive`, `computed`, `watch`. Two-way binding: `v-model`. Directives: `v-if`, `v-for`, `v-on:click` (or `@click`), `v-bind` (or `:`). Companion libs: Vue Router, Pinia (state, replaces Vuex), Nuxt (meta-framework like Next.js).

Angular: opinionated TypeScript framework by Google. Components with decorators (`@Component({ selector, template, styleUrls })`), services with `@Injectable`, dependency injection, modules, RxJS observables for async, Angular CLI for scaffolding. Steeper learning curve than React/Vue. Strong fit: large enterprise apps where opinionated structure helps. Signals (v17+) added for finer-grained reactivity.

Svelte: compiler that turns components into vanilla JS at build time — no virtual DOM, no runtime framework. `.svelte` files: `<script>let count = 0</script><button on:click={() => count++}>{count}</button>`. Reactivity: `$:` for derived values. Stores for shared state. SvelteKit: full-stack meta-framework (like Next.js for Svelte). Tiny bundles, fast runtime.

Vite: modern dev server and build tool. Dev: serves source via native ES modules — instant startup, blazing HMR. Build: uses Rollup for optimized production bundles. Replaces Webpack for most new projects. Config: `vite.config.js`. Built-in: TypeScript, JSX, CSS modules, PostCSS, env vars. Plugin ecosystem mirrors Rollup. Created by Evan You (Vue author) — works with React, Vue, Svelte, vanilla.

Webpack: classic JS bundler. Concepts: entry, output, loaders (transform files: babel-loader, css-loader), plugins (HtmlWebpackPlugin, DefinePlugin), code splitting, tree shaking. Dev: webpack-dev-server with HMR. Config-heavy (`webpack.config.js`). Replaced for most new projects by Vite/esbuild/Turbopack, but still common in legacy and very customized setups.

Babel: JavaScript compiler. Transpiles modern JS (ES2020+, JSX, TypeScript) into JS that older browsers understand. Presets: `@babel/preset-env` (targets via browserslist), `@babel/preset-react`, `@babel/preset-typescript`. Plugins for proposals (decorators, etc). With ES2020+ supported in 95%+ of browsers, many projects now skip Babel in favor of esbuild/swc/Vite's native transforms.

ESLint: pluggable static analysis for JS/TS. Config: `.eslintrc` or `eslint.config.js` (flat config). Rules: errors, warnings, fixable. Common configs: eslint-config-airbnb, eslint-config-standard, eslint:recommended. Plugins: react, react-hooks, jsx-a11y, import, @typescript-eslint. Run: `eslint .` or `--fix`. Combine with Prettier (formatting) — eslint-config-prettier disables conflicting rules.

Prettier: opinionated code formatter. Few options: print width, tab width, single quotes, trailing commas, semi. `.prettierrc` for config. Run on save (editor plugin) or pre-commit (husky + lint-staged). Pairs with ESLint: Prettier handles formatting, ESLint catches bugs. Solves bikeshedding about style — pick the default and move on.

Jest: JS testing framework (Meta). Features: zero-config for most projects, snapshot testing, mocks, coverage. Syntax: `describe('user', () => { test('greets', () => { expect(greet('A')).toBe('hi A') }) })`. Async: `await` or `done` callback. Mocks: `jest.fn()`, `jest.mock('./module')`, `jest.spyOn(obj, 'method')`. Modern alternative: Vitest — Jest-compatible API, faster, uses Vite.

Cypress: browser-based E2E testing. Runs in a real browser, with time-travel debugging. `cy.visit('/login'); cy.get('#email').type('a@b.com'); cy.contains('Sign in').click(); cy.url().should('include', '/dashboard')`. Auto-waits for elements (no flaky setTimeouts). Limitations: same-origin only (until recent versions), Chromium-family browsers (Firefox supported but less common).

Playwright: Microsoft's E2E testing tool. Multi-browser (Chromium, Firefox, WebKit), parallel by default, auto-waiting, network interception, mobile emulation, video recording. `await page.goto('/'); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click()`. Codegen: `playwright codegen` records your actions as test code. Generally faster and more capable than Cypress for cross-browser needs.

Web accessibility (a11y): make sites usable by everyone, including screen readers, keyboard-only users, low vision. Use semantic HTML first (button vs div with onClick). ARIA fills gaps: `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-hidden`, `role` (only if no semantic equivalent). Keyboard: all interactive elements must be focusable and have visible focus. Contrast: 4.5:1 for normal text. Test: axe DevTools, Lighthouse, manual keyboard nav.

SEO basics: descriptive `<title>` (50-60 chars), `<meta name='description'>` (150-160 chars), one `<h1>`, semantic HTML, alt text on images, fast load time (Core Web Vitals), mobile-friendly, HTTPS, structured data (schema.org JSON-LD), clean URLs, sitemap.xml, robots.txt. Content quality + backlinks matter more than meta tweaks. For SPAs: prerender or SSR so crawlers see content.

Web perf: minimize JS bundle (code split, tree shake, dynamic import), defer non-critical CSS/JS, lazy-load images (`loading='lazy'`), serve modern formats (WebP, AVIF), use CDN, enable HTTP/2 or 3, cache aggressively (immutable + content hash in filename), preload critical fonts, avoid layout shifts. Measure: Lighthouse, WebPageTest, real user monitoring (Google CrUX, Sentry, Datadog).

Core Web Vitals (Google ranking factors): LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, <2.5s) — when main content loads; CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, <0.1) — visual stability; INP (Interaction to Next Paint, <200ms, replaced FID) — responsiveness. Improve LCP: optimize hero image, preload critical resources. Improve CLS: reserve space for images/ads, avoid injecting content above existing. Improve INP: break up long tasks, defer non-critical JS.

Chrome DevTools tabs: Elements (inspect DOM/CSS, live edit), Console (logs, run JS), Sources (debugger, breakpoints, blackboxing), Network (waterfall, throttling, request inspection), Performance (CPU profiling, flame chart), Memory (heap snapshots, leaks), Application (storage, service workers, manifest), Lighthouse (audits). Shortcuts: Cmd+Opt+I (open), Cmd+P (jump to file), Cmd+Shift+P (command menu).

Chrome extension: `manifest.json` (v3) declares name, version, permissions, action (toolbar button), background (service worker), content_scripts (run in page context). MV3 uses service workers (no persistent background page). APIs: chrome.tabs, chrome.storage, chrome.runtime, chrome.scripting. Load unpacked: chrome://extensions → Developer mode → Load unpacked. Publish: $5 one-time developer fee, review can take days.

Express: minimal Node.js web framework. `const app = express(); app.use(express.json()); app.get('/users/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id })); app.listen(3000)`. Middleware: `(req, res, next) => { ... next() }`. Error middleware has 4 args: `(err, req, res, next)`. Common middleware: cors, helmet (security headers), morgan (logging), express-rate-limit. Modern alternatives: Fastify (faster), Hono (edge-friendly), Koa.

Flask: microframework for Python. `from flask import Flask; app = Flask(__name__); @app.route('/'); def home(): return 'hi'; app.run()`. Routes with vars: `/users/<int:id>`. JSON: `from flask import jsonify`. Request data: `request.json`, `request.args`, `request.form`. Templates: Jinja2 (`render_template`). Production: never `app.run()` — use gunicorn behind nginx. Extensions: Flask-SQLAlchemy, Flask-Login, Flask-WTF.

Django: batteries-included Python web framework. ORM, admin panel, auth, forms, templates, migrations all built in. MTV pattern (Model-Template-View). Start: `django-admin startproject myproj; python manage.py startapp blog`. Models → migrations: `makemigrations` then `migrate`. Powerful admin: register a model and get a CRUD UI for free. DRF (Django REST Framework) for APIs. Heavier than Flask but huge ecosystem.

FastAPI: modern Python web framework, async-first, type-hint driven. `@app.get('/users/{id}'); def get(id: int) -> User: ...`. Auto-generated OpenAPI docs at `/docs` (Swagger UI) and `/redoc`. Pydantic validates request/response models. Async support: `async def` route handlers. Fast (Starlette + Uvicorn). Great for APIs; for full apps with templates, Flask/Django might fit better.

Ruby on Rails: convention-over-configuration full-stack Ruby framework. MVC (Models, Views, Controllers). Generators: `rails new blog; rails generate scaffold Post title:string body:text`. ActiveRecord ORM. Migrations: `db/migrate/*.rb`. Strong opinions = fast development for CRUD apps. Famous for: DHH, Basecamp, GitHub, Shopify (still on Rails at massive scale). 'Hotwire' (Turbo + Stimulus) for SPA-like UX without much JS.

Laravel: PHP framework heavily inspired by Rails. Eloquent ORM, Blade templates, Artisan CLI (`php artisan migrate`), Composer for packages. Features: auth scaffolding, queues, broadcasting, scheduled tasks. Companion tools: Forge (deploy), Vapor (serverless), Nova (admin), Livewire (Phoenix LiveView for PHP — server-rendered reactive UIs). The most popular modern PHP framework.

Go: statically typed, compiled, garbage-collected (Google, 2009). Simple syntax, fast compile times, great concurrency. Goroutines: `go fn()` — lightweight threads. Channels: `ch := make(chan int); ch <- 1; v := <-ch`. Interfaces: implicit (any type implementing methods satisfies). Std lib is rich (net/http, encoding/json). `go mod init`, `go build`, `go test`. No exceptions — errors are returned values. No generics until 1.18.

Rust: systems language with memory safety without GC. Ownership model: each value has one owner; borrowing rules checked at compile time. No null, no data races. `let mut x = 5;`, `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 { a + b }`. Result/Option for errors and absence. Cargo for build/deps. Async via tokio. Steep learning curve (the borrow checker), but huge wins in performance and correctness. Powers Firefox, Discord backends, ripgrep, parts of Linux kernel.

Spring Boot: opinionated Java/Kotlin framework. Auto-configures common pieces. `@SpringBootApplication` on main class. `@RestController` + `@GetMapping('/users')` for HTTP endpoints. Dependency injection via `@Autowired` or constructor. Spring Data JPA for repositories. `application.properties` or `application.yml` for config. Maven or Gradle build. Start with Spring Initializr (start.spring.io). Heavy but battle-tested for large enterprise systems.

ASP.NET Core: Microsoft's cross-platform web framework (C#). Minimal APIs (since .NET 6): `app.MapGet('/users/{id}', (int id) => new { id })`. Or MVC with controllers and views. Built-in DI, configuration, logging, auth (Identity). EF Core ORM. Razor Pages for server-rendered. Blazor for full-stack C# (WASM or Server). Generally very fast (TechEmpower benchmarks).

GraphQL server: define schema (typeDefs) + resolvers. Schema-first with Apollo Server: `type Query { user(id: ID!): User }`. Resolvers: `Query: { user: (_, { id }) => db.user(id) }`. Code-first: schema generated from TS/Python code (Nexus, Strawberry). N+1 problem: use DataLoader to batch + cache lookups. Federation: combine multiple GraphQL services into one. Many teams have moved back to REST/tRPC for simplicity.

REST API design: resources as nouns (`/users`, `/posts/123/comments`), HTTP verbs as actions (GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH update, DELETE remove). Status codes: 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirect, 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429), 5xx server error (500, 502, 503). Versioning: URL (`/v1/users`) or header. Pagination: cursor (stable) > offset (skips on inserts). HATEOAS rare in practice.

WebSocket server: Node's `ws` library: `new WebSocketServer({ port: 8080 }).on('connection', ws => { ws.on('message', m => ws.send('echo: ' + m)) })`. Socket.IO adds: auto-reconnection, rooms, namespaces, fallback to long-polling, ack callbacks. Other ecosystems: ws (Node), websockets (Python), Phoenix Channels (Elixir, brilliant for scale), SignalR (.NET). Scale horizontally: pub/sub via Redis or NATS to share messages across instances.

Session auth: server creates a session, stores in DB/Redis, sends session ID to browser as HttpOnly cookie. Browser sends cookie automatically on every request. Pros: easy revocation (delete session), no token-in-storage XSS risk. Cons: server-side state, scaling needs shared store. CSRF risk → use SameSite=Lax cookies and/or CSRF tokens. Set: Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (no JS access), SameSite=Lax|Strict.

JWT: signed token containing claims (user id, expiry, etc) in base64-encoded JSON. Format: `header.payload.signature`. Signed (HS256 with secret, or RS256 with private/public keys). Pros: stateless, works across services. Cons: hard to revoke before expiry (need a blocklist), payload is readable (not encrypted), large for cookies. Common mistake: storing in localStorage (XSS-exposed) — prefer HttpOnly cookie.

OAuth2: delegated authorization. Common flows: Authorization Code (web apps with backend; use PKCE), Authorization Code + PKCE (SPAs, mobile), Client Credentials (server-to-server), Device Code (TVs, CLIs). NOT for authentication on its own — pair with OpenID Connect (OIDC) which adds an id_token. Providers: Google, GitHub, Auth0, Okta, Clerk. Never roll your own — too easy to get subtly wrong.

RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): users get roles (admin, editor, viewer), roles have permissions, code checks `user.has_permission('post.delete')`. Simpler than ACLs (per-resource permissions) but less flexible. ABAC (Attribute-Based): dynamic rules based on user/resource/context. PBAC/policy-based: rules in code (OPA/Rego, Cedar, Casbin). For most apps: start with RBAC, add resource-level checks where needed.

Middleware: function in the request/response pipeline. Pattern: `(req, res, next) => { /* before */ next(); /* after */ }`. Order matters — registered first runs first on the way in, last on the way out. Use for: logging, auth, body parsing, CORS, rate limiting, error handling. Skip downstream by not calling next(). Express, Koa, FastAPI, Rails (`before_action`), Django all have middleware.

Rate limiting: cap requests per IP/user/key. Algorithms: token bucket (steady rate, allows bursts), leaky bucket, fixed window (counter resets every interval — boundary spikes), sliding window (smoother). Storage: Redis with INCR + EXPIRE. Headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `-Remaining`, `-Reset`, `Retry-After`. Status: 429. Layer at edge (Cloudflare, nginx) AND app (per-user limits). Higher limits for authenticated users.

Redis: in-memory key-value store. Data structures: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets (leaderboards), hashes, streams. Pub/sub. TTL on any key. Persistence: RDB (snapshots), AOF (append-only log), or both. Use cases: caching, sessions, rate limiting, queues, leaderboards. Single-threaded → atomic operations, no lock concerns. Cluster mode for sharding. Alternative: Valkey (fork after license change), KeyDB (multi-threaded fork).

RabbitMQ: message broker implementing AMQP. Producers send to exchanges, exchanges route to queues, consumers pull from queues. Exchange types: direct (routing key match), topic (pattern match), fanout (broadcast), headers. Acknowledgments: consumer must ack or message requeues. Persistent messages survive broker restart. Use for: decoupling services, retries, fan-out, async workers. Alternatives: Kafka (log-based, replay), NATS (lightweight).

Apache Kafka: distributed event streaming platform. Topics → partitions → ordered logs. Producers append, consumers read by offset. Unlike a queue: messages aren't deleted on read; multiple consumer groups can read same topic independently. Retention by time or size. Use cases: event sourcing, analytics pipelines, microservice communication, log aggregation. Heavyweight to operate — managed offerings: Confluent Cloud, AWS MSK, Redpanda (Kafka-compatible).

Webhooks: outbound HTTP POSTs your server sends when events occur, vs the client polling. Receiver should: verify signature (HMAC of body with shared secret), respond 2xx quickly (do work async), be idempotent (same event might arrive twice), tolerate out-of-order delivery. Common: Stripe, GitHub, Slack. For local testing: ngrok or webhook.site.

Background jobs: offload slow work (emails, image processing, API calls) from the request cycle. Job queue stores tasks; workers pull and execute. Ecosystems: BullMQ (Node + Redis), Sidekiq (Ruby + Redis), Celery (Python + Redis/RabbitMQ), Resque, Inngest, Trigger.dev (managed). Features to want: retries with backoff, dead-letter queue, scheduled jobs, concurrency limits, observability.

File uploads: HTML form `<input type='file'>` posts `multipart/form-data`. Server: Express → `multer`, Flask → `request.files`. Large files: stream to disk/S3, don't buffer in memory. Direct-to-S3 uploads with presigned URLs save your server's bandwidth. Validate: file size, MIME type (don't trust extension), scan for malware on untrusted input. Resumable uploads: tus protocol.

Sending email: don't run your own SMTP server (deliverability hell). Use a provider: Postmark (transactional), SendGrid, AWS SES (cheap), Resend (developer-friendly), Mailgun. Setup: SPF + DKIM + DMARC DNS records — all three or your mail goes to spam. Use a dedicated sending domain. Separate transactional (receipts, password resets) from marketing (newsletters). Test deliverability: mail-tester.com.

PDF generation: HTML-to-PDF is the practical path. Node: Puppeteer (headless Chrome) → `page.pdf()`. Python: WeasyPrint (pure CSS, no JS), pdfkit (wkhtmltopdf wrapper), ReportLab (programmatic). Server-side concerns: Chrome eats RAM (use a pool or hosted service: Browserless, DocRaptor, Gotenberg). Forms with input: pdf-lib (Node) or PyPDF2 to fill existing PDF templates.

Image processing: Node — `sharp` (libvips, fast), `jimp` (pure JS, slow). Python — Pillow, OpenCV. CLI — ImageMagick (`convert`, `magick`). Common ops: resize, crop, compress, format conversion (JPEG/PNG/WebP/AVIF), strip EXIF, watermarks. For user-uploaded images: always re-encode (strips malware embedded in metadata), limit dimensions, use modern formats.

Elasticsearch: distributed search engine built on Lucene. Indexes documents, fast full-text + structured search. Concepts: index (like DB), document (like row), mapping (schema), analyzer (tokenization). Query DSL is JSON. Aggregations for analytics. Often pairs with Kibana (visualization) + Logstash/Beats (ingestion) = ELK stack. Alternatives: OpenSearch (AWS fork), Meilisearch (smaller, simpler), Typesense, Algolia (hosted).

Pagination patterns: offset/limit (`LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40`) — simple but slow on big tables and skips/duplicates on inserts; cursor/keyset (`WHERE id < ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20`) — fast and stable but no random page jumps. Use cursor for infinite scroll/timelines, offset for admin tables with page numbers. Always order by a unique tiebreaker.

Database connection pooling: opening a Postgres connection is slow (~10-50ms). Pool keeps connections open and reuses them. App-level pool (per process). For serverless or many app instances: connection multiplier — PgBouncer, Supabase pooler, RDS Proxy. Modes: session (sticky, allows prepared statements), transaction (better reuse but limits), statement (most reuse, fewest features).

ORM vs raw SQL: ORMs (Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM, SQLAlchemy, ActiveRecord) give type-safety and ergonomics but can generate slow queries (N+1) and hide what's happening. Raw SQL (or query builders like Kysely, knex) is more explicit but boilerplate-heavy. Pragmatic: use ORM for simple CRUD, drop to raw SQL for complex reports and performance-critical paths. Always log generated queries in dev.

DB migrations: versioned schema changes checked into source control. Each migration: up (apply) + down (reverse). Tools: Flyway, Liquibase, Knex, Prisma Migrate, Alembic (Python), Active Record migrations (Rails). Rules: never edit a migration after it's deployed — write a new one. Backwards-compatible deploys: add column nullable → deploy code → backfill → make NOT NULL. Test migrations on prod-shaped data.

DB seeds: populate dev/test databases with predictable data. Pattern: `seed.js` script that inserts a set of users, posts, etc. Idempotent: clear or upsert so reruns work. Faker/Mockaroo for realistic dummy data. For tests: factories (factory-bot, factory_boy, fishery) build fresh objects per test. Don't seed prod from the same script — separate one-off scripts for prod data backfills.

DB transactions: group operations as atomic unit. `BEGIN; UPDATE...; UPDATE...; COMMIT;` or `ROLLBACK;`. Isolation levels: Read Uncommitted (dirty reads), Read Committed (default in Postgres), Repeatable Read, Serializable (strongest, slowest). Phenomena: dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read. Long transactions hold locks → cascading slowdowns. Keep them short.

ACID properties: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (transitions valid states only), Isolation (concurrent txs don't interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes). Classic relational DBs (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) are ACID. Many NoSQL trade ACID for scale/availability — eventually consistent. Modern NewSQL (CockroachDB, Spanner, TiDB) try to give ACID at horizontal scale.

SQL vs NoSQL: SQL (Postgres, MySQL) — relational, schema-enforced, JOINs, strong consistency, mature. NoSQL — schema-flex, often horizontally scalable, varies wildly: document (MongoDB), key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j). Modern Postgres handles JSON, full-text, vectors — covers most NoSQL use cases. Choose NoSQL for clear reasons (massive write scale, specific data model), not hype.

MongoDB: document database. Collections of BSON documents. Schema-flex. `db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 18 } })`. Indexes (regular, compound, text, geo). Aggregation pipelines: `$match`, `$group`, `$lookup` (join-ish). ACID transactions within a replica set. Sharding for horizontal scale. Use cases: rapid prototyping, content with varying shapes. Critique: many former Mongo users have moved to Postgres + JSONB.

PostgreSQL: open-source, feature-rich relational DB. ACID, advanced types (arrays, JSON/JSONB, ranges, UUID), full-text search, extensions (PostGIS for geo, pgvector for AI, TimescaleDB for time-series, pg_cron). Foreign keys, CTEs, window functions, triggers, materialized views. Defaults to row-level locking for high concurrency. The 'just use Postgres' default for new projects. Hosted: Supabase, Neon, Render, RDS.

MySQL: classic open-source RDB, owned by Oracle since 2010. MariaDB is the community fork. InnoDB engine: row-level locking, ACID, foreign keys. Widely used (LAMP stack, WordPress). Postgres generally has more features and a cleaner spec; MySQL has historically had better replication tooling. Use MySQL when ecosystem demands (WordPress hosts), otherwise Postgres is usually the safer default for new projects.

SQLite: serverless, file-based SQL database. One file, no daemon, ACID. Used in: every phone, every browser, most desktop apps. Surprisingly capable for small-to-medium server apps too (Litestream replicates the file to S3 for backup; LiteFS for distributed). Limit: concurrent writers serialize. New 'just use SQLite' movement for indie web apps — fast and simple.

DynamoDB: AWS managed NoSQL key-value + document. Single-table design pattern: store many entity types in one table using composite keys (PK + SK). Strong consistency optional per read. Auto-scales reads/writes. No JOINs, limited query patterns — design access patterns upfront. Pricing: pay per read/write unit or on-demand. Great for serverless (Lambda); painful when access patterns change.

Cassandra: distributed wide-column store, written at Facebook, open-sourced. Linear horizontal scaling, no single point of failure, multi-datacenter replication. Eventually consistent (tunable per query). Wide rows: very efficient for time-series and write-heavy workloads. Painful operations and modeling (must design around access patterns). Used by Netflix, Discord, Apple.

DB indexes: B-tree (default, range + equality), hash (equality only), GIN (full-text, JSONB, arrays in Postgres), GiST (geometric, geographic). Speeds up reads, slows down writes. Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY. Composite indexes match left-to-right (an index on (a,b) helps `WHERE a=? AND b=?` and `WHERE a=?` but not `WHERE b=?`). EXPLAIN to verify usage. Don't over-index — every index has write cost.

Query optimization: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows the plan and actual times. Look for: seq scans on large tables (need index), nested loops with high row counts (better as hash join), filter on big result set (move filter into the index). Common fixes: add index, rewrite to use existing index, limit result set earlier, denormalize hot read paths, batch queries to avoid N+1, use partial indexes for sparse data.

N+1 problem: 1 query to fetch parents, then N queries to fetch each parent's children. ORMs make this easy to do accidentally. Fixes: eager loading (`include`/`with`/`joinedload` — JOINs the children in), DataLoader pattern (batches lookups in GraphQL), explicit SQL with JOINs. Always log queries in dev so you spot N+1 before it ships.

Sharding: split data across multiple DB instances. Shard key (user_id, tenant_id) determines which shard a row lives on. Pros: ~unlimited horizontal scale. Cons: cross-shard queries are painful, joins limited, rebalancing is hard, ops complexity high. Last resort — first try vertical scaling, read replicas, caching, partitioning. Managed: Citus (Postgres extension), Vitess (MySQL), Spanner, CockroachDB.

Replication: copy data from primary to replicas. Sync (waits for replica ack — slower writes, safer) vs async (faster but lag). Use replicas for: read scaling, reporting, geographic distribution, failover. Watch out for replica lag — reads-after-writes from the primary, not the replica, or accept eventual consistency. Multi-primary is hard; most setups are single-primary with read replicas.

DB backups: full + incremental. Test restore regularly — an untested backup is not a backup. Off-site/off-account copies (a compromised account can delete in-account backups). Retention: align with RPO/RTO. Postgres: pg_dump for logical, pg_basebackup + WAL for PITR (point-in-time recovery). Managed: RDS snapshots, Litestream for SQLite. Encrypt at rest. Document the restore procedure — practice it.

Disaster recovery: planning for catastrophic loss. RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data loss is acceptable (e.g., 5 minutes). RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long until restored (e.g., 1 hour). Strategies (cheapest to costliest): backup + restore (high RTO), pilot light (minimal standby), warm standby, hot standby/multi-region. Run game days — simulate failure and recover.

Serverless functions (FaaS): write a function, provider runs it on demand, pay per invocation. AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers, Vercel Functions, Netlify Functions. Pros: no servers to manage, scales to zero, fast deploy. Cons: cold starts, time limits (~15min Lambda, much shorter on edge), stateful tasks awkward, vendor lock-in. Sweet spot: HTTP APIs, scheduled jobs, event handlers.

AWS Lambda: runs your function in response to events (HTTP via API Gateway/Function URL, S3 upload, SQS message, CloudWatch schedule). Languages: Node, Python, Go, Java, Ruby, .NET, custom runtimes. Cold start: ~100-500ms (longer for JVM/.NET). Mitigate: provisioned concurrency, smaller bundles, faster runtimes. Pricing: per invocation + GB-second of memory/time. Often paired with DynamoDB, S3, API Gateway.

Vercel: hosting platform from Next.js creators. Push to GitHub → automatic preview deployments per PR + production deploys on merge.
