Examples: `0 * * * *` (every hour), `*/15 * * * *` (every 15 min), `0 2 * * *` (2 AM daily), `0 0 * * 0` (Sunday midnight). Capture output: `>> /tmp/job.log 2>&1`. Gotchas: minimal PATH, no shell init, no $HOME by default. Modern alternative: systemd timers (better logging, deps, calendar specs).

Webhook security: verify HMAC signature header (Stripe, GitHub, Slack include one). Compute HMAC-SHA256 of raw body with your shared secret; compare in constant time. Use raw body bytes, not parsed JSON (parsing rounds-trips can change bytes). Reject if timestamp is too old (replay protection). Don't trust headers from untrusted callers — IP allowlists less useful than HMAC.

Postgres JSONB: binary-stored JSON, indexable, queryable. `CREATE TABLE events (id serial, data jsonb)`. Query: `data->>'name'` (text), `data->'addr'->>'city'`, `data @> '{"type":"click"}'` (contains). GIN index for fast containment: `CREATE INDEX ON events USING gin(data jsonb_path_ops)`. Generally prefer columns for known fields, JSONB for the variable tail.

Postgres extensions: PostGIS (geo), pg_trgm (fuzzy text search), pgvector (AI embeddings), TimescaleDB (time-series), pg_stat_statements (query stats), pg_cron (in-DB scheduled queries), pg_partman (partition management), hstore (key-value). `CREATE EXTENSION name`. Check available: `SELECT * FROM pg_available_extensions`. Most managed Postgres providers offer common ones.

pgvector: Postgres extension for vector similarity search. `CREATE EXTENSION vector; CREATE TABLE items (id int, embedding vector(1536))`. Insert with embeddings from OpenAI/Cohere/local model. Query: `SELECT * FROM items ORDER BY embedding <=> '[...]' LIMIT 5`. Indexes: IVFFlat (faster build, recall tradeoff), HNSW (more memory, better recall). Pairs with Postgres full-text + structured data — usually no need for separate vector DB at small/medium scale.

Redis pub/sub: publishers send to channels, subscribers receive. `PUBLISH chan 'hi'`, `SUBSCRIBE chan`. No persistence — subscribers offline at publish time miss messages. For durable messaging, use Redis Streams instead. Use pub/sub for: cache invalidation across instances, live notifications, lightweight broadcast. For replay/durability/consumer groups: Streams (`XADD`, `XREADGROUP`).

OpenAI API: `from openai import OpenAI; client = OpenAI(); response = client.chat.completions.create(model='gpt-4o', messages=[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}])`. Stream: `stream=True`, iterate chunks. Tools (function calling) via `tools` param. Vision: include image_url in message content. Embeddings: `client.embeddings.create(model='text-embedding-3-large', input=text)`. Anthropic, Google, Mistral, etc. have similar APIs — many SDK-compatible.

Anthropic API (Claude): `from anthropic import Anthropic; client = Anthropic(); msg = client.messages.create(model='claude-sonnet-4-6', max_tokens=1024, messages=[{'role':'user','content':'hi'}])`. Tools: pass `tools=[...]` with JSON schemas, Claude returns `tool_use` blocks. Streaming: `stream=True`. Multimodal: text + image in content array. Long context: up to 200k tokens (1M on selected models). Caching for repeated context.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): retrieve relevant context from a knowledge base, pass to LLM as part of prompt. Pipeline: chunk docs → embed → store in vector DB → at query time, embed query, find top-k, stuff into prompt. Improvements: hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vector), reranking (cross-encoder), query rewriting, citations in output, chunking strategies (semantic chunking, parent-child).

Prompt engineering: be specific (role, task, format, constraints), use examples (few-shot — show 2-5), structure with markdown (headers, lists), ask for step-by-step reasoning ('think step by step'), specify output format (JSON schema, code block). For complex tasks: decompose into sub-prompts, use chain-of-thought. Iterate empirically — small wording changes have large effects. Eval set + automated scoring beats vibes.

LLM tool use (function calling): give the model a list of functions with JSON schemas; it decides when to call them and produces structured arguments. Loop: send messages → model returns tool_use → you execute → return tool_result → model uses output to continue. Pattern enables: search, calculation, API calls, code execution. Anthropic and OpenAI both support; format differs slightly but concept identical.

LangChain: framework for composing LLM apps. Provides: model wrappers, prompt templates, output parsers, chains (sequential ops), agents (tool-using loops), memory, document loaders, vector stores. Reputation: powerful but heavyweight and abstraction-heavy — many devs prefer direct API calls + small libraries. Alternatives: LlamaIndex (RAG focus), Haystack, simple custom code. Use the right tool for your complexity level.

MCP (Model Context Protocol, Anthropic 2024): open standard for connecting LLMs to tools/data sources. Server exposes tools, resources, prompts; client (e.g., Claude Desktop, Claude Code) uses them. Transport: stdio (local) or SSE/HTTP (remote). Build a server in any language (TS/Python SDKs official). Lets you build once and use in any MCP-compatible client. Gaining wide adoption in late 2024/2025.

Vector embeddings: dense numeric representations of text/images/audio where similar items are close in vector space. Cosine similarity or dot product for comparison. Models: OpenAI text-embedding-3 (paid, strong), Cohere, voyage-3, open: sentence-transformers, BGE, nomic-embed, mxbai-embed-large. Dimension: 384-1536 typical. Trade-offs: smaller dim = cheaper storage/search; larger = better recall.

Docker compose example: `services:
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: dev }
    volumes: ['db_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data']
  api:
    build: .
    depends_on: [db]
    environment: { DATABASE_URL: postgres://postgres:dev@db:5432/postgres }
    ports: ['3000:3000']
volumes: { db_data: {} }`. Run: `docker compose up -d`, logs: `compose logs -f api`.

12-Factor App (Heroku, 2011): cloud-native app principles. Codebase (one repo, many deploys), Dependencies (declare explicitly), Config (in env), Backing services (treat as attached resources), Build/release/run (separate), Processes (stateless), Port binding (self-contained), Concurrency (process model), Disposability (fast start/stop), Dev/prod parity, Logs (event streams to stdout), Admin processes. Still mostly correct decades later.

Semantic Versioning (SemVer): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for backwards-compatible features, PATCH for fixes. Pre-release: 1.0.0-beta.1. Build metadata: 1.0.0+sha. SemVer-range in npm: `^1.2.3` (any 1.x.x ≥ 1.2.3), `~1.2.3` (1.2.x). Pre-1.0: anything goes (0.x). Critique: most projects don't truly follow it; minor bumps break things.

Keep a Changelog: write CHANGELOG.md by hand (or generated). Sections per version (newest first): Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write for humans, not machines — describe what users care about, not commit list. 'Unreleased' section at top for pending changes. Tools: changesets, release-please, semantic-release for automation.

API versioning: URL path (`/v1/users` — simple, visible), header (`Accept: application/vnd.api.v1+json` — clean URLs, hidden from logs), query param (`?version=1`). Versionless API with field deprecation: GitHub-style, requires great communication. Breaking change strategy: ship new endpoint, deprecate old with sunset date, monitor usage. Don't break URLs in v1 forever — assume someone is depending on them.

Feature flags: ship code behind switches; toggle without redeploy. Use for: gradual rollouts, kill switches, A/B tests, internal vs external, dark launches. Tools: LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook (OSS), Unleash (OSS), PostHog, Statsig, ConfigCat. Cleanup is critical — old flags accumulate. Tag each flag with owner + expected removal date. Don't nest flag checks; flags create branching paths in code that must be tested.

Test doubles: stubs (return canned data), mocks (verify interactions), spies (record calls), fakes (working but simplified — in-memory DB), dummies (placeholders). Mock at boundaries (HTTP, DB, time, random); don't mock your own code. Over-mocking → tests pass while code is broken. Prefer integration tests with real dependencies in containers (testcontainers) when feasible.

TDD (Test-Driven Development): red (write failing test), green (minimum code to pass), refactor (clean up while green). Forces small steps, design through tests. Pros: regression safety, design pressure (testable code is decoupled), confidence to refactor. Cons: slower in unfamiliar domains, mocked-heavy tests can be brittle. Pragmatic: TDD where requirements are clear; spike + test for exploratory work.

SOLID principles (Robert Martin): Single Responsibility (one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification), Liskov Substitution (subtypes substitutable for base), Interface Segregation (many small interfaces > one fat), Dependency Inversion (depend on abstractions). Useful checklist, not gospel. Easy to over-apply — small classes everywhere bury logic in indirection. Apply when complexity warrants.

DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself, Hunt & Thomas): every piece of knowledge has a single, unambiguous representation. Critique: overapplied. Don't dedupe coincidental similarity — when two things may evolve differently, duplication is freer. WET (Write Everything Twice) and 'rule of three' (extract abstraction after third repetition) are sane refinements.

YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): don't build features until needed. Future-proofing usually doesn't match actual future needs. Hypothetical flexibility creates real complexity now. Counter-balance: leave hooks where extending is highly predictable. The most expensive code is code you wrote that's never used — and it slows you down forever.

KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): simpler designs win — fewer bugs, easier handoff, easier change. Complexity should justify itself. Symptoms of over-engineering: speculative generality, premature abstraction, deep inheritance, too many layers. Constraint = creativity. The simplest thing that could possibly work, then iterate. Rich Hickey's 'Simple Made Easy' is great companion reading.

MVC (Model-View-Controller): Model (data + domain logic), View (UI), Controller (mediates input → model → view). Origin: Smalltalk-80. Modern web: Rails, Django, Spring define MVC differently than original. React isn't really MVC — it's component-based with one-way data flow. MVVM, MVP are related variants. Pattern names obscure as much as they clarify.

Functional programming: emphasize pure functions, immutability, functions as values, expressions over statements, composition. Languages: Haskell (pure, lazy), Erlang/Elixir (concurrency), F#, Clojure (Lisp on JVM), OCaml. Multi-paradigm languages with strong FP support: Scala, Rust, Swift, modern JS/TS. Concepts: higher-order functions, currying, recursion + tail calls, algebraic data types (sum + product), pattern matching.

Why learn programming? Automate repetitive tasks. Build things others can use. Understand the increasingly digital world. Career flexibility — software touches every industry. Strong problem-solving skill that transfers. Joy of creation — turning ideas into working things from text. Accessible: free tools, free tutorials, vast community. Hard but worth it.

Starting to code: pick one language (Python is the gentlest, JavaScript if you want web). One project (something you want), not endless tutorials. Build, search when stuck, repeat. freeCodeCamp, The Odin Project, CS50 (Harvard, free). Code daily even briefly — consistency beats intensity. You'll feel stupid often — that's normal and necessary. Cycle through 'I get it' → 'I don't get it' → 'I get it' forever.
